architecture_summary: A literary mystery in which every accurate map takes a memory that returns only through a licensed renewal, so knowledge is a debt that can be inherited and a permission that can be refused. Wonder at the coast becomes dread as the cost moves through the surveyor's family line; hope depends on a renewal someone could refuse or be denied.
open_questions: Whose memory should the final record preserve, and who decides?
Is the Guild's lie ever defensible as mercy, or only as control?
Should the city's founding crime be public knowledge or a private grief?
How much of the surveyor's own past may the story erase before she is no longer the same person?
Who may renew a memory on another person's behalf, and at what cost?
Is a returned memory the same memory, or a reconstruction the family accepts?
Can a family appeal a Guild refusal to renew?

creative_intentions.title: Renewal-bound restorative discovery
creative_intentions.directive: Discovery should become restorative through chosen renewal: keep the wonder-to-dread movement, but let hope depend on someone renewing a debt they could refuse.

adopted_creative_alternative.author_question: Keep the wonder-to-dread movement and the conditional hope. The recorded relation says the memory economy turns every discovery into a personal loss. Give me materially different mechanisms by which that cost could be borne or returned, each changing its operating rules and consequences rather than its name.
adopted_creative_alternative.description: A memory is returned only if the same resident renews the survey each season. If they cannot, the debt passes to their family line. Operating rule: recovery is conditional and renewable. Consequence: dread shifts from sudden erasure to an obligation that children inherit, and hope depends on someone choosing to renew rather than on a single act of mercy.
adopted_creative_alternative.title: Renewal-bound debt

hypotheses.title: Inheritance as theme
hypotheses.description: If the debt is inherited rather than only personal, the story's theme shifts from what a community owes its dead to what a household owes for a choice it did not make. That is a different thematic centre, not merely a stronger version of the old one.

uncertainties: Whether the wider cost weakens the intimate horror cannot be decided from the candidate; it needs drafted scenes.
The proposal adds an open question about who may renew on another person's behalf, and the answer would change the dilemma's fairness.
Reader experience remains an interpretation of intended effects, not an observed response.

superseded_inquiry_history.author_question: Take the renewal-bound debt alternative: a memory returns only if the same resident renews the survey each season. What must the story keep unresolved so that inherited debt reads as a tragic obligation rather than a simple punishment?
superseded_inquiry_history.analysis: The referent is present in this request: the earlier explore answer lists h1 Renewal-bound debt, whose operating rule is that a memory returns only if the same resident renews each season, with the debt passing to the family line otherwise. To keep inherited debt tragic rather than punitive, three questions must stay unresolved on the page. First, whether anyone can renew on another person's behalf, and at what cost to their own record. Second, whether a refusal is honoured when the refusal itself endangers the household. Third, whether a returned memory is the same memory or a reconstruction that the family accepts as true. If the story answers all three early, the debt becomes a rule to be obeyed and the dread turns into punishment. If it keeps them contested, dread stays inside the family's own reasoning about obligation.
uncertainties: The candidate does not record whether memories can be renewed, transferred or reconstructed, so the answer depends on an unrecorded rule.
Whether readers experience inherited obligation as tragic or punitive is not established by any recorded field.

hypotheses.title: Consent ledger
hypotheses.description: Each contributor must consent per survey, and a refusal is recorded and honoured, so the archive grows thin exactly where people refused. Operating rule: the payer decides each time. Consequence: dread becomes civic and uneven, and the mystery must work around honest gaps rather than a single hidden crime.

hypotheses.title: Concealed cost
hypotheses.description: The cost is paid but never announced in the city; the reader infers it from names that stop appearing and from records that do not add up. Operating rule: disclosure, not allocation. Consequence: dread comes from inference, so the first erasure lands as a pattern the reader notices before the surveyor does.

uncertainties: The candidate does not record who currently pays for the Guild's surveys, so each alternative changes an unrecorded fact.
Reader effects are interpretations of intended effects and must be tested against drafted material.
